video_title: Going Ballistic - The Ballistic Missile Resurgence From Ukraine to Iran & the Pacific
gist: Conventional ballistic missiles are having a 2020s resurgence because better sensors and networks reward fast, hard-to-intercept response weapons, and because the wars in Ukraine and Iran-Israel have shown both their battlefield value and the impossibility of purely defensive counters; Russia's Iskander, China's DF-26/Fire Dragon family, US PrSM, Turkey's Tayfun/Samsun, and South Korea's Hyunmoo 5 illustrate very different national bets, while NATO Europe scrambles from a near-standing start.

themes.theme: History & the core rationale for ballistic missiles

insights.claim: Germany's WWII V2 program illustrates the enduring drawback of ballistic missiles: expensive, technically unreliable delivery of a one-off quantity of explosive with poor accuracy against point targets, even though it produced real casualties at scale (roughly 3,100 V2s launched from Oct 1944, with ~1,365 fired at London killing ~2,700 civilians and ~1,664 fired at Antwerp killing ~1,700, but the missiles reportedly almost never hit specific point targets like dock gates or bridges).
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: The core economic weakness of ballistic missiles — expensive per-shot, weak against precise point targets — has been a constant since 1944 and still shapes how militaries value them today.

insights.claim: Post-Cold War, most NATO militaries (including the US Army with ATACMS) let ballistic missile production lines go cold and deprioritized long-range strike generally, while Russia, China, Iran and North Korea kept investing and modernizing their arsenals — a divergence now driving NATO's catch-up scramble.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Explains why Western defense-industrial capacity for ballistic missiles is comparatively thin today and why current European rearmament programs are effectively starting from near-zero industrial base.

insights.claim: Ballistic missiles' three enduring attractions versus alternatives are reach, speed (Iranian missiles reportedly reach Israel in about 12 minutes versus roughly 2 hours for cruise missiles and up to 9 hours for drones), and industrial accessibility — building a capable ballistic missile force is comparatively far easier than fielding a modern strategic bomber fleet or aircraft carrier.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: This is why resource-constrained actors like Iran and North Korea gravitate to ballistic missiles as their best available long-range coercive tool rather than air power or naval projection.

insights.claim: Defending against ballistic missiles requires not just expensive interceptors but the specialized sensors, cueing systems, and trained crews to use them correctly, and nations that lack any of these are largely left with hoping for luck ("HP tanking") as their main defense.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Missile defense is a systems problem, not just an interceptor-count problem, which raises the effective cost and difficulty of achieving real protection.

themes.theme: Why ballistic missiles are resurging in the 2020s

insights.claim: The proliferation of space-based sensors, drones, and networked military hardware has made a real 'kill web' increasingly achievable, and this puts a premium on weapon systems that can respond quickly to fresh targeting data — a role ballistic and hypersonic missiles are well suited to fill.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Sensor and networking progress, not just missile technology itself, is a primary driver of renewed ballistic missile investment across multiple militaries.

insights.claim: Ballistic missile accuracy has improved sharply from historic CEPs measured in hundreds of meters or kilometers to some modern systems claiming single-digit or low-double-digit meter CEP, aided by in-flight course correction and terminal-phase sensor packages like imaging infrared seekers.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Better accuracy is expanding the practical target set for ballistic missiles well beyond area bombardment, including against moving targets like ships.

insights.claim: Anti-ship ballistic missiles are becoming a genuine multi-national trend rather than a novelty: China has invested heavily in the category, South Korea is developing one for its multiple rocket launcher, and the US and Turkey have both conducted test firings of ballistic missiles against naval targets.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Surface warships, previously considered relatively safe from ballistic missile threats, now face a widening set of potential attackers with this capability — a significant naval-planning consideration.

insights.claim: Cluster-munition-equipped ballistic missiles have performed very differently depending on the target: they wrecked an entire Russian helicopter base in a handful of ATACMS shots and have proven useful against soft Russian battlefield targets, but Iran's cluster-armed strikes on Israel were largely ineffective because sheltered populations meant the bomblets caused little real damage — turning an expensive delivery system into what the narrator calls "a multi-million dollar delivery system for a bunch of hand grenades."
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Cluster payloads are highly target-dependent: excellent against exposed battlefield assets or airbases, poor as a strategic bombardment weapon against sheltered populations or hardened structures.
insights.quote: what you're essentially looking at is a multi-million dollar delivery system for a bunch of hand grenades

insights.claim: Iran's ballistic missile campaign against Israel and US bases produced mixed but non-trivial results: it did little large-scale damage to Israeli civilian infrastructure, but scored hits on US military bases, destroyed some assets, forced allies to expend thousands of PAC-3 interceptors, and — via a strike on Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG facility — caused significant economic disruption despite most missiles being intercepted.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: A country with Iran's modest resource base was able to meaningfully stress US/allied missile-defense magazines and impose real economic damage, which is a strong procurement argument for other resource-limited states considering ballistic missiles.

themes.theme: Russia's Iskander becomes Ukraine's hardest air-defense problem

insights.claim: Ukrainian sources claim Russia has ramped Iskander-M production to roughly 60 units per month, a large figure by global standards, though Russian commanders would reportedly still prefer more.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: This production rate underpins Russia's sustained ability to conduct both tactical strikes and a strategic bombing campaign against Kyiv simultaneously.

insights.claim: A Ukrainian estimate from June 2025 put Iskander production at more than 700 units over the prior 12 months, roughly 3x the estimate for the year before, with further (if less dramatic) increases reported by Ukrainian officials in 2026.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: The compounding growth rate in Iskander output is straining Ukraine's PAC-3 interceptor stocks, which the narrator says are close to exhaustion ("fairly close to Winchester").

insights.claim: Russia has reportedly deprioritized production of the air-launched Kinzhal (Dagger) hypersonic missile, and Ukrainian sources say the freed components and fuel have been redirected to boost Iskander production instead — consistent with Kinzhal's practical drawback that the carrier aircraft's takeoff gives Ukraine advance warning, eroding the missile's speed advantage.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Russia appears to be reallocating resources away from a hyped but operationally compromised hypersonic system toward its most effective ground-launched tactical missile — a real-world signal about which capability actually delivers value in this war.

insights.claim: Production of Russia's large Kh-32 cruise missile (a Kh-22 modernization) is reportedly halted while production of the much smaller Bandera mini cruise missile has ramped up, suggesting a broader Russian shift toward smaller, more numerous strike weapons.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: A move toward smaller, cheaper strike weapons alongside surging Iskander output suggests Russia is optimizing for mass and saturation of Ukrainian air defense rather than per-unit sophistication.

insights.claim: Russia has reportedly modernized Iskander along three axes — scaling production, increasing range, and improving its ability to punch through modern air defenses, including countermeasure modules that deploy decoys during the missile's terminal phase.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Even as Ukraine gains access to more capable Western air-defense systems, the threat itself is becoming simultaneously more numerous and more evasive, keeping the interception problem hard.

insights.claim: Unlike US or Chinese pod-based launcher systems that can quickly swap between different missile types, Russia's Iskander launchers are single-role — they fire either the Iskander-M ballistic missile or the Iskander-K cruise missile but can't be rapidly reconfigured — meaning an opponent who locates one has more certainty about the threat it poses, a rare instance of Russian design conservatism versus the ambiguity built into Western/Chinese "loot box" launcher systems.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Launcher modularity is itself a tactical variable: pod-based systems create deliberate ambiguity for the opponent that Russia's current design does not exploit.

insights.claim: China's DF-26 is a roughly 20-ton, ~4,000km-range missile (in service since 2016) carrying a 1,200-1,800kg conventional or nuclear warhead — with 4,000km being enough range to hit US bases on Guam, hence its media nickname the "Guam killer"; an anti-ship variant has also reportedly been tested.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: DF-26's range and reported anti-ship capability is a direct driver behind long-standing (and still largely unmet) calls for the US Air Force to build hardened shelters on Guam.

insights.claim: China's JL-1 air-launched ballistic missile, recently shown off, would let China's comparatively old, non-stealthy strategic bomber fleet strike distant targets without needing to approach close to well-defended airspace.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Air-launched ballistic missiles are a way for China to extend the relevance of an aging bomber fleet without requiring a new stealth bomber program.

insights.claim: China's Fire Dragon 480 is a smaller, pod-based tactical ballistic missile roughly comparable to ATACMS/PrSM, with claimed anti-shipping capability; a 2024 Chinese-media-reported simulation claimed just six Fire Dragon 480s plus a drone swarm and new tactics were enough to overwhelm and sink a simulated Ticonderoga-class cruiser in the Red Sea, but this result should be treated skeptically since it is an unverifiable, non-repeatable claim released by an interested party.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Chinese-sourced simulation claims about sinking US warships should not be taken as predictive evidence without independently verifiable assumptions, even though they do signal Chinese interest in ballistic missiles as an anti-ship saturation tool.

insights.claim: China is reportedly working toward real-time tracking of surface combatants from space, paralleling US Air Force arguments that IMTI satellites could replace some AWACS functions for tracking aircraft — both examples of the sensor infrastructure that makes fast-reacting weapons like ballistic missiles more valuable.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Real-time space-based maritime tracking would materially close the sensor-to-shooter loop needed to make Chinese anti-ship ballistic missiles operationally effective against moving targets.

themes.theme: America's PrSM bet and the Iran-war burn rate

insights.claim: Reuters reported (Aug 4) that the US used virtually all of its long-range precision missiles — specifically ATACMS and PrSM — during the war against Iran, with US commanders apparently valuing these capabilities enough to use them extensively even when other options existed.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Rapid depletion of ATACMS/PrSM stockpiles in one regional conflict raises real questions about US precision-munition inventory depth for a larger or simultaneous contingency (e.g., against China).
insights.quote: US has used virtually all of its long-range precision missiles during the Iran war, sources say

insights.claim: PrSM is designed to trade warhead mass for precision and launcher density: it fits two missiles per HIMARS/M270 pod versus one ATACMS, while claiming more range than the older ATACMS it replaces.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: The US design philosophy bets that precision and volume of fire can substitute for raw payload mass — the opposite bet from Turkey's or South Korea's much larger missiles.

insights.claim: PrSM's planned increments add new seekers (enabling ship targeting), alternative warhead/payload options including a loitering-munition delivery mode, and — at Increment 4 — a ramjet propulsion upgrade extending range to about 1,000km (enough for a Ukraine-to-Moscow shot), with Increment 5 aiming to make it launchable from an autonomous platform.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: The roadmap shows the US consolidating multiple future mission sets (anti-ship, loitering-munition truck, deep strike, autonomous launch) into a single evolving missile family rather than fielding separate bespoke systems.

insights.claim: During the Iran war the US reportedly used ATACMS/PrSM against a range of targets including submarines at dock, indicating a willingness to expend high-end precision munitions against high-value fixed targets.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Using scarce, expensive precision missiles against static high-value assets like submarines-at-dock signals how highly US planners value those specific target types even at high inventory cost.

themes.theme: Europe's scramble to rebuild sovereign strike capability

insights.claim: NATO announced a roughly $50 billion, UK-led push for European deep precision strike capability at the July 2026 summit, deliberately spread across multiple programs rather than concentrated in a single missile design, aimed at building sovereign long-range coercive capability that doesn't depend on asking another country for permission to strike.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: A $50B multi-program approach signals NATO Europe treats sovereign long-range strike as a strategic gap urgent enough to fund broadly rather than bet on one winner.
insights.quote: Share expertise, technology advances, and deepen industrial cooperation to rapidly advance NATO capabilities.

insights.claim: The UK's Project Nightfall — a relatively affordable tactical ballistic missile originally meant largely for transfer to Ukraine — had its target specs relaxed after "feedback from industry representatives," from a 600km range/300kg warhead/~$670k unit cost down to 500km/200kg/~$1M per shot, with only a minimum production rate of about 10 missiles per month initially planned.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: The spec downgrade and modest production target show the real-world difficulty and cost of standing up an affordable ballistic missile industrial base essentially from scratch, even for a program explicitly designed to be simple and cheap.

insights.claim: The UK has separately allocated about a quarter of a billion dollars to buy US PrSM for its own army (500km range), but because PrSM is ITAR-controlled, the UK cannot freely transfer it to allies like Ukraine — its only options are to seek US permission or fire the missiles themselves.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Buying American gives faster capability but locks in US veto power over onward transfer — a direct rationale for the UK simultaneously pursuing the ITAR-free, transferable Project Nightfall.
insights.quote: the only two ways for the United Kingdom to transfer them to another state will be to either seek US mission or fire them

insights.claim: Germany's Rheinmetall has announced plans to produce ATACMS in Europe — the first time this system has been manufactured outside the United States — though it remains a design generation behind current US systems and Washington retains significant control as the licensor.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: European localization of US missile production is happening, but it's starting with older-generation designs and doesn't fully remove US leverage over the supply chain.

insights.claim: Concentrating NATO's long-range strike capability in only a few member states (many not on the alliance's eastern flank) creates a geopolitical risk: Moscow could potentially manage an escalation more favorably by pressuring only the small set of states holding escalatory tools to blink, rather than facing a uniformly capable alliance — making broader distribution of these weapons across NATO members a deterrence-strengthening goal in itself.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: This reframes European ballistic/strike-missile proliferation within NATO not just as capability-building but as a deliberate hedge against Russia exploiting asymmetric escalation-control leverage.

themes.theme: Turkey's rapidly scaling ballistic missile program

insights.claim: Turkey scored a public export success with a ~280km-range tactical ballistic missile sold to Indonesia (announced 2022, deliveries commencing 2025), demonstrating Turkey's emergence as a credible ballistic missile exporter.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Turkey is becoming a viable alternative supplier of tactical ballistic missiles alongside the US and South Korea for countries seeking options outside those two.

insights.claim: Turkey's larger Tayfun missile entered service in 2023, and a Block 3 test firing earlier in 2026 reportedly scored a precise hit on a small, moving boat target — a technically demanding feat for a ballistic missile.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: This puts Turkey among the small group of countries (with China, South Korea, the US) actively demonstrating anti-ship ballistic missile capability, not just testing it conceptually.

insights.claim: Turkish ballistic missiles are scaling up dramatically in size: the Block 4 Tayfun concept shown in 2025 is roughly 10m long, 940mm in diameter, and 7.2 tons, versus the early Block Typhoon's ~6.5m/610mm/2.3 tons, alongside a separate Samsun medium-range ballistic missile (per IISS assessment, ~2,000km range, unveiled 2023) and a conceptual conventionally armed ICBM with a commonly cited range of about 6,000km.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Turkey's trajectory (go bigger) is the opposite design philosophy from the US PrSM approach (go smaller/more precise), illustrating there is no single dominant global design paradigm for conventional ballistic missiles.

insights.claim: The narrator is skeptical that Turkey's conceptual conventional ICBM makes coherent military sense against Turkey's likely regional adversaries, since those targets don't require intercontinental range — suggesting prestige, political signaling, or civilian space-launch program spillover as more plausible drivers than an actual operational requirement.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Not every high-profile missile program reflects genuine operational logic — some may be better explained as prestige projects or dual-use space technology development.

themes.theme: South Korea's Hyunmoo 5 and the economics of a bunker-buster missile

insights.claim: South Korea's Hyunmoo 5 is a roughly 36-ton road-mobile ballistic missile carrying a reported ~8-ton (17,000lb) warhead — versus a 'typical' conventional ballistic missile's roughly 2,200lb warhead and the prior Hyunmoo 4's 4,400lb — meaning the Hyunmoo 5 warhead alone reportedly outmasses five entire ATACMS missiles combined.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: This is an outlier design globally — most of the warhead mass is believed to be hardened bunker-busting casing rather than explosive filler, built for a specific deep-target-defeat mission against North Korea.

insights.claim: Hyunmoo 5 was only possible after a 2017 agreement with the United States lifted prior restrictions on South Korean missile range and warhead mass, a policy change that followed North Korea's hydrogen bomb test.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: North Korea's 2017 nuclear test indirectly enabled South Korea's subsequent heavy conventional ballistic missile buildout by triggering the removal of alliance-imposed constraints.

insights.claim: Compared to the US Massive Ordnance Penetrator (a reusable-aircraft-delivered, gravity-dropped 14-ton bomb with ~2 tons of explosive filler), Hyunmoo 5 delivers a similarly large hardened warhead via a one-shot ballistic trajectory that likely arrives faster than terminal velocity from a drop, but expends the entire (much more expensive) delivery vehicle each time rather than reusing an aircraft — trading unit economics for full national sovereignty and the ability to skip building a strategic bomber force or US-style air force entirely; reported range flexes from roughly 600km with the heaviest bunker-busting payload up to several thousand kilometers with a lighter payload, enough to reach most of China, all of Japan, and parts of Russia.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: For a country unwilling or unable to build a strategic bomber force, a heavy ballistic missile is a capital-intensive but achievable substitute path to deep-strike capability, consistent with South Korea's broader defense preference for capital over manpower given its demographics.

insights.claim: The narrator floats two under-discussed hypotheticals: (1) if South Korea ever pursued independent nuclear weapons, Hyunmoo 5 or a Korean SLBM could serve as a ready-made strategic delivery system requiring only a warhead to be added; and (2) a similar heavy, sovereign, conventionally armed ballistic missile could appeal to a European state such as Poland seeking independent deterrence capability against Russia, potentially complicating Moscow's escalation calculus.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Flags a plausible but unconfirmed proliferation and export pathway worth watching: heavy conventional ballistic missiles as both a latent nuclear-delivery hedge and a potential new export category for European sovereign-deterrence buyers.
insights.quote: giving someone like Poland a small cluster of 30-plus ton delete buttons seems like the kind of thing that might prompt an interesting statement or three from Lavrov

insights.claim: Even the wealthiest, best-funded militaries cannot rely on missile defense alone against ballistic and hypersonic threats — interceptors are extremely expensive relative to the missiles they counter, offensive technology keeps improving, and the investment required for total (or even major) defense coverage is typically prohibitive, meaning credible sovereign offensive/strike capability has to be part of any serious deterrence posture.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: This is the episode's central strategic conclusion and directly justifies the wave of Western and allied investment in offensive strike systems (PrSM, Nightfall, Tayfun, Hyunmoo 5) rather than defense-only postures.

insights.claim: Access to meaningful long-range strike capability is becoming increasingly 'democratized' — available not only to resource-constrained actors like Iran and North Korea but now to individual members within alliances like NATO, without requiring the industrial base for a bomber force or carrier fleet.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: More independent actors gaining credible long-range strike options changes escalation dynamics broadly, not just in traditional great-power confrontations.

insights.claim: The war in Ukraine suggests combining cheap one-way-attack drones with ballistic missiles produces better results than relying on ballistic missiles alone, likely because the combination saturates and complicates the defender's air-defense prioritization.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Force-mix design matters as much as any single weapon's specs — cheap drones and expensive ballistic missiles are complementary, not substitutes, for saturating modern air defense.

insights.claim: Ballistic missiles give political leaders a tool to conduct demonstrative or limited strikes without risking a crewed aircraft or personnel, fitting a broader 21st-century pattern of conflict that is often neither clearly 'shooting war' nor clearly 'peace,' with ballistic missiles playing an escalation-management and pressure role short of all-out war.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Ballistic missiles may increasingly be used as a signaling/coercion tool in gray-zone confrontations rather than purely as war-fighting weapons, a distinct use case procurement planners should account for.

insights.claim: Ballistic missiles' deterrent value is inconsistent across cases: South Korea explicitly frames Hyunmoo 5 as a deterrence tool, yet Iran's large conventional ballistic missile arsenal did not deter recent military action taken against Iran — the same general weapon category produced opposite deterrence outcomes.
insights.speaker: narrator/host
insights.so_what: Investors and analysts should be cautious about assuming ballistic missile arsenals automatically confer deterrence; outcomes appear to depend heavily on the broader strategic context, not the weapon alone.
